A comparative analysis of the language, structure, and drafting conventions of EU Regulations and Directives -- the two pillars of Union legislative action.

Key Drafting Patterns

Direct Obligations

Regulations address actors directly:

  • "The manufacturer shall draw up the technical documentation."
  • "ESMA shall establish a register."
  • "The determining authority shall examine applications."

Definitions Article

Article 2 (or 3), invariant syntax:

  • "'[term]' means [definiens];"
  • Genus-differentia (most common)
  • Cross-reference to other acts
  • 18-74 definitions per act

Delegation of Powers

Two distinct mechanisms:

  • Delegated acts (Art 290): supplement/amend non-essential elements
  • Implementing acts (Art 291): uniform conditions, comitology
  • RTS/ITS for financial services (agency-drafted)

The Defining Pattern: "Member States Shall Ensure"

This construction is the single most distinctive linguistic feature of directives. It creates binding obligations while preserving Member State implementation freedom.

ECN+ (2019/1)

* Design Protection Directive uses substantive-declarative provisions instead ("A design shall be considered new if...")

The Transposition Article

Standard Formula

"Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive by [DATE]."

  • Tripartite formula: "laws, regulations and administrative provisions"
  • Result obligation: "necessary to comply" -- not verbatim transposition
  • Deadline: Typically 2-3 years after adoption
  • Notification: "They shall immediately inform the Commission thereof"

Variations

  • Split deadlines: phased implementation for specific articles
  • Two-date structure: adoption deadline + later application date
  • Recast-selective: only new/amended provisions require transposition
  • Communautaire reference: national law must cite the directive
  • Communication obligation: text of main national measures sent to Commission

Harmonisation Spectrum

MINIMUMFULL (MAXIMUM)
Floor-setting
Flexible
Prescriptive
Ceiling

Minimum Markers

  • "at least" / "at a minimum"
  • "without prejudice to"
  • "shall not preclude Member States"
  • "more stringent" / "more extensive"
  • "higher level of protection"
  • Non-regression clause

Full Harmonisation Markers

  • "shall not maintain or introduce provisions diverging from"
  • Absence of "at least" and "may provide"
  • Substantive-declarative style
  • Direct rules without flexibility

JHA/Schengen-Specific Features

Variable Geometry

  • Protocol 21: Ireland opt-in/opt-out
  • Protocol 22: Denmark permanent opt-out
  • Schengen: Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Liechtenstein association

Legal Bases

  • Art 82(2) TFEU -- criminal procedure
  • Art 83 TFEU -- criminal law
  • Art 87(2) TFEU -- police cooperation

Non-Regression Clause

Four-tier protection floor: EU Charter, ECHR, international law, more protective national law.

Comparative Analysis

Side-by-side examination of structural, linguistic, and functional differences.

Fundamental Differences

FeatureRegulationDirective
Legal Effect Directly applicable, no transposition Requires national transposition
Enacting Formula "HAVE ADOPTED THIS REGULATION:" "HAVE ADOPTED THIS DIRECTIVE:"
Closing Clause "Binding in its entirety and directly applicable" "This Directive is addressed to the Member States"
Core Obligation Pattern "The authority shall..." "Member States shall ensure that..."
Rights Creation Direct: rights conferred on individuals Indirect: via MS obligations
National Flexibility Minimal -- prescribes directly Significant -- "in accordance with national law"
Transposition Article Absent Present (always, with tripartite formula)
Addressee Clause Absent "This Directive is addressed to the Member States"
Variable Geometry Rare (typically universal) Common in JHA (Protocol 21/22)
Typical Size 50-113 articles, 75-110 recitals 25-50 articles, 40-80 recitals
Definitions 18-74 (more detailed) 3-22 (defers to national law)

Shared vs. Unique Elements

Shared by Both

  • Title block format
  • Preamble (visas) sequence
  • Modal verb hierarchy
  • "Whereas:" + numbered recitals
  • Chapter > Section > Article hierarchy
  • Definitions article ("means" copula)
  • Cross-referencing system
  • Delegated/implementing acts
  • Subsidiarity recital
  • Entry into force formula
  • Review clause

Regulation-Only

  • "Binding in its entirety" clause
  • "Directly applicable" language
  • Direct rights creation
  • Higher definition count (18-74)
  • Larger article count (50-113)
  • CE marking / notified bodies
  • RTS/ITS (financial services)
  • Staggered application dates

Directive-Only

  • Transposition article
  • "Addressed to the Member States"
  • "Member States shall ensure" pattern
  • Minimum/full harmonisation markers
  • Non-regression clause
  • Variable geometry (JHA)
  • Explanatory documents recital
  • Correlation table (recast)

Amendment Technique (Shared)

Amendment Instructions

  • "Article X is replaced by the following:"
  • "Article X is amended as follows:"
  • "the following article is inserted: Article Xa"
  • "the following points are added:"
  • "Article X is deleted;"

Alphanumeric Convention

Inserted provisions use letter suffixes to preserve parent numbering:

  • Articles: 5a, 5b, 5c...
  • Paragraphs: 1a, 1b, 2a...
  • Points: (5a), (23a), (23b)...

"Inserted" = between existing items. "Added" = at the end.

Practical Guidance for Brubru Users

When Amending a Regulation

  • Use "shall" for obligations, "may" for permissions -- never "must" or "should" in operative text
  • Address actors directly: "The provider shall..."
  • Cross-reference: "as referred to in Article X(Y)"
  • Definitions: "'[term]' means [definiens];"
  • Use alphanumeric suffixes for insertions (Art 5a)

When Amending a Directive

  • Use "Member States shall ensure that..." for result obligations
  • Include "in accordance with national law" for implementation details
  • Add "at least" for minimum harmonisation floors
  • Include realistic transposition deadlines
  • Remember: you set the result, not the exact national rules
